{"answer":"Start with short, predictable sessions and stop before your dog gets overwhelmed. Use a soft brush, let them sniff it first, then pair each touch with treats or a lick mat so the brush predicts something good. Brush in the spots they tolerate best first, keep the pressure light, and work in small sections with breaks. If they hate the brush on their skin, try a grooming glove or a comb with wider spacing, and make sure any tangles are worked out gently instead of pulling.\n\nIt also helps to brush after exercise or a calm walk, when they’re less keyed up. {"answer":"Don’t make him vomit unless a vet or poison hotline tells you to. {"answer":"Start very small and make alone time feel predictable. Begin by leaving the dog for just a few seconds while they’re calm, then come back before they get upset. Repeat that a lot, and slowly stretch the time over days or weeks. Pair departures with something good and quiet, like a stuffed Kong or chew that they only get when you leave, then pick it up when you return.\n\nKeep arrivals and departures low-key, and practice at times when the dog is already relaxed rather than after a burst of excitement. If the dog starts pacing, barking, scratching, or panicking, you’ve moved too fast, so shorten the next practice session. A crate can help some dogs, but only if they already feel safe in it. The goal is calm confidence, not forcing them to be alone longer than they can handle.","answerSections":[{"heading":"What helps most","items":["Use tiny absences at first, then build up
